19703-madame-delphine:
George W. Cable wrote about Creole New Orleans with unmatched local knowledge. Madame Delphine is one of his best-known stories of that city. Its opening shows a quarter sunk into long decay. Old commercial glory has shrunk into small shops. Bright market stalls stand out like patches of mould. Cable sets mood before he sets plot in motion.

Cable's New Orleans tales deal with caste, color, and old French families. Madame Delphine stands at the center of such a tale. Her story turns on sacrifice within a rigid social order. Cable wrote the city's speech and streets from life. His work helped define Southern local-color fiction. This short novel remains a fine place to meet it.
19779-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-20-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1867 is volume 20, number 118 of the magazine. One essay here treats grief with striking practicality. Grief, it says, must be fed with thought or starve to death. The best plan is keeping the mind busy with other work. The essay calls busyness a spiritual anesthetic for sorrow. Such counsel filled postwar American magazines.

The Civil War had ended two years before this issue. Its readers knew bereavement at national scale. The Atlantic mixed essays, fiction, and reviews for educated households. A single issue preserves the era's whole mental diet. Scholars read such numbers to hear 1867 thinking aloud. This one speaks in a Boston accent, thoughtful and composed.
19939-history-of-the-missions-of-the-ame:
This history covers missions of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Its ground is the Ottoman world: Armenians, Greeks, and the Turkish empire. In March 1846, Sir Stratford Canning reported from Constantinople. Thirty-six evangelical Armenians stood persecuted by their Patriarch, he wrote. Canning added personal efforts to soften their treatment. Diplomacy and missions intertwine through the narrative.

The American Board sent its first missionaries abroad in 1812. Its Near East missions built schools, presses, and colleges. Armenian converts stood at the center of this volume's story. Persecution reports shaped American sympathy and policy. The history is both record and advocacy. Scholars of missions still work through its documents.
19941-with-our-army-in-palestine:
John Morecroft wrote With Our Army in Palestine about the British campaign there. He corrects the home public's short version of that war. Most people think the Great Crusade began with taking Jerusalem, he says. They think it ended when the Turks surrendered in autumn 1918. That view is entirely erroneous, he insists. The campaign was longer, wider, and harder than the famous dates suggest.

Palestine saw fighting from Gaza to Damascus over two years. Allenby's army mixed British, Indian, Australian, and Arab forces. Morecroft marched with them as an official observer and writer. His book restores the campaign's full length. Desert, water, and distance are its real antagonists. It is solid campaign history from a participant.
19996-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for October 1865 is volume 16, number 96. The Civil War had ended six months before this issue. One article attacks a fashionable claim about American health. Physical decay, it is said, threatens the American people. Unwise stimulation of the brain gets the blame. A deficiency of physical health in America is assumed as an axiom. The writer questions that assumption sharply. Postwar nerves were a national topic that autumn.

The magazine now spoke for a victorious, grieving Union. Its pages balanced reconstruction politics with science and letters. Health anxiety ran through much postwar writing. This article shows the argument in its first form. A single number captures the culture re-sorting itself. Scholars still read these volumes as America's diary.
20071-sue-a-little-heroine:
L. T. Meade wrote Sue, A Little Heroine, one of her many books for young readers. Sue is a small girl with a freckled face and red-tinged hair. Her eyes are bright blue and keen, the book notes at once. She pushes through a crowd to hear a street preacher speak.

A rough man lays a hand on her shoulder in that crowd. From such small scenes, Meade builds a tale of a brave child. Sue faces hard city life with faith and pluck. Readers get a Victorian tale of poverty, courage, and a child's good heart under strain.
20263-boswell-s-correspondence-with-the-:
James Boswell's correspondence with Andrew Erskine appears here with notes by George Birkbeck Hill. Hill praises a young Scot who dared to tour Corsica's interior. No traveler from Britain had visited that interior before him. Turkish corsairs still swarmed the Mediterranean in that risky age.

Corsica itself sat in a very unsettled state at the time. Boswell's letters show his wit, ambition, and love of great men. Erskine, a poet and soldier, proved a bright partner in letters. Readers get lively eighteenth-century correspondence, richly framed by a top editor.
20340-a-little-maid-of-old-maine:
Alice Turner Curtis wrote A Little Maid of Old Maine, a tale of the Revolution. Two girls carry a big basket toward the Machias River in Maine. It is a pleasant May morning in 1775, full of pine scent. Freshly cut logs have been poled downriver to the big sawmills.

War news from Lexington has just reached the Maine coast that spring. Machias would soon fight one of the first naval battles of the war. Curtis sets her little maid amid lumber, ships, and patriots. Young readers get Maine's own Revolution story, told at a child's height.
20378-christmas-sunshine:
Christmas Sunshine is a seasonal gift book of verse and readings for the Christmas season. Its pages mix classic religious poetry with pieces on winter, snow, and the birth of Christ. The selection suits family reading by the fireside.

One passage praises winter as it hides the bare earth under innocent snow. It speaks of a saintly veil of maiden white thrown over the year's shame. Such lines show the book's mix of nature writing and devotion, and the warmth its makers hoped to bring into the home at Christmas.
20496-legends-of-the-rhine:
Legends of the Rhine brings the old tales of Germany's great river to English-speaking readers. Castles, knights, water spirits, and doomed lovers crowd its pages. The book mixes travel talk with the legends themselves, in the manner of a journey up the river.

One scene has a young woman smile at a compliment to her mother. The mother, it turns out, was English by birth. The traveler remarks that Germany is the land of romance for the English, just as Italy is for the Germans. The legends that follow show why the Rhine earned that name.
20513-how-to-succeed-or-stepping-stones-:
Orison Swett Marden's How to Succeed, published in 1896, is one of the founding books of the success movement. Its full title promises stepping stones to fame and fortune. Marden told young readers that will and character, not luck, make a life.

Do not look far for the successful man, he writes. This man is you, it is I, it is each one of us. How do we constitute ourselves men? Nothing is harder if we do not know how to will it, and nothing easier if we will it. Such bracing talk made Marden's books steady sellers.
20616-the-old-front-line:
John Masefield walked the Somme battlefield soon after the fighting and wrote The Old Front Line about what he found. Masefield had served in France and wrote with a poet's eye. The book describes the trenches, villages, and graves of the 1916 battle.

He looks ahead to peace. The ground full of death will grow food again, he writes, and this frontier of trouble will be forgotten. When the trenches are filled in and the plough has gone over them, the land will not long keep the look of war. The book became a classic of battlefield writing.
21027-the-trial-of-charles-random-de-ber:
False word of peace with France, spread to lift the funds, charges the Crown in this trial. Charles de Berenger, Lord Cochrane, and others stood accused of that fraud in 1814. The Trial records a plot to make the king and public believe peace was near.

Stock Exchange fraud, a fake colonel, and a staged ride from Dover fill the case. Cochrane, a sea hero, swore his innocence to his death's door. The verdict wrecked his career, though later ages cleared his name in part. Trial reports like this preserve court drama word for word, cross-talk, proof, and all.
21119-flaming-june:
A tidy elderly spinster in a seaside town keeps a large house. It has private access to a shared garden, and her settled life is upset by a visitor. Her brother, now rich in America, sends his daughter Cornelia to England as part of her education. Cornelia arrives with plenty of pocket money and American habits.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey sets the girl among polished, well-bred people who expect chaperones and strict manners. Cornelia gads about with young men as she pleases, to her aunt's dismay. The aunt proves right in the end: among all the nice people hides one bad character, revealed only near the close.
21250-sir-walter-scott-a-lecture-at-the-:
William Paton Ker delivered this lecture on Sir Walter Scott at the Sorbonne on May 22, 1919, in the Louis Liard series. He takes his text from Scott's own account of seeing Ivanhoe turned into an opera at the Odéon in Paris. Scott, who dictated much of that novel in pain at Abbotsford, marvelled that it now amused a foreign crowd.

Ker contrasts Scott's regional Scotland, its dialect barely clear outside its own ground, with the Europe-wide market that fought for his novels. The lecture first appeared in the Anglo-French Review in August 1919. It is a short, warm weighing of Scott's European fame.
21273-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-2-no-1:
The Atlantic Monthly for December 1858, volume two, number fourteen, opens with an essay on the ideal tendency in art. Its writer argues that art is the largest expression, pointing toward what cannot be measured or lodged in systems. Shakespeare, Plato, Michelangelo, Beethoven, and Goethe stand as its witnesses.

The young Atlantic, founded in Boston the year before, aimed to lead American letters, art, and politics in one magazine. A single monthly number like this one mixes essays, stories, poems, and reviews by the New England circle. Kept whole, it shows the magazine in its second year, when its table of contents was itself an argument about American culture.
21288-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for March 1866, volume seventeen, number 101, leads with passages from Hawthorne's notebooks, published two years after his death. One entry describes a July 1837 drive near Augusta, Maine, to fish for white perch through a crooked, winding brook. The pilot talks politics and the bank between hearty tugs at a whiskey bottle.

Several dozen fish, yellow perch, a great chub, and horned pouts come home in an hour or two. Ticknor and Fields published the magazine in Boston as a monthly of literature, science, art, and politics. A single issue preserves its post-Civil War table, where Hawthorne's private journals shared space with the day's essays.
21325-outlines-of-greek-and-roman-medici:
James Sands Elliott was a New Zealand doctor and editor of the New Zealand Medical Journal. He wrote these outlines after a stay in southeastern Europe stirred his interest. Published in 1914, the book traces the main stages of healing in the Greek and Roman worlds. Those are the two empires to which modern civilisation owes most. Asklepios, the Greek god of healing, fronts it.

Elliott complains that the history of medicine is much neglected, even by doctors, so that many discoveries are only rediscoveries. He keeps the book a general outline rather than a full treatise, leaning on German historians like Baas and Sprengel. It serves as a short, readable first map of ancient medicine.
21408-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The April 1866 number of the Atlantic Monthly, volume seventeen, number one hundred and two, leads with the last days of Walter Savage Landor. Landor had died at Florence in September 1864, and many readers barely knew his name. The piece asks why so bright a writer was so little read.

The Atlantic was then a leading magazine of letters, science, art, and public life. Its pages mixed essays, reviews, poems, and tales for a broad, keen readership. This number preserves a slice of that world just after the Civil War. Emerson's own account of Landor, from English Traits, is quoted and weighed.
21572-percival-keene:
Percival Keene grows up near Southampton in Captain Marryat's novel of 1842, his nineteenth book. An old mansion house, known by its name for centuries, stands a few miles from the town. Sea service, in the channel frigate world of the day, shapes the hero's path.

Channel service, Marryat jokes, meant a captain with a seat in Parliament. His frigate rarely went to sea while the House was sitting, lest his vote be missed. Against that sly background, young Keene learns the navy as it truly was. Love, patronage, and action fill a tale told with Marryat's usual pace and humour.
21642-lady-cadogan-s-illustrated-games-o:
Lady Cadogan's Illustrated Games of Solitaire, in a new revised edition of 1914, adds American games. David McKay of Philadelphia issued the book, under the motto that patience conquers. A line from Othello asks how poor are they that have not patience.

Terms come first: foundation cards, suitable cards, and marriage, meaning a card placed on its neighbour in suit. Games run from Canfield, or Klondike, to Napoleon at St Helena and the Besieged City. La Belle Lucie, the Flower Garden, and the Sultan crowd the long contents list. Players get clear rules and pictures for dozens of single-player card games.
21716-the-battery-and-the-boiler-adventu:
A baby born at sea in a howling storm grows up to work with the newest wonder of his age in this Ballantyne tale. The boy's early squalls mark him, the ship's cook jokes, as one who will make his mark somehow. He finds his chance in the laying of submarine telegraph cables, the wires that first linked lands across the oceans.

Ballantyne studied cable laying firsthand, as he did for many of his books on trades and crafts. Storms, ships, sparks, and mishaps fill the story, mixing sea adventure with early electrical work. Readers get a lively look at the crews who strung the world's first ocean telegraph lines.
22058-cornelius-o-dowd-upon-men-and-wome:
Charles Lever, the Irish novelist, created Cornelius O'Dowd as a comic mask for his magazine essays. The pieces first ran in Blackwood's Magazine and were gathered in book form in 1864. O'Dowd introduces himself as a man who waited fourteen years at levees for government favour. No viceroy ever gave him a post, which leaves him free to talk.

From Italian battlefields to Dublin drawing rooms, O'Dowd comments on everything. Garibaldi's worshippers, Solferino, Italian law, and organ grinders all come under his eye. The humour is broad, Irish, and topical. Readers in the 1860s took these papers as light relief with a sting.
22090-the-task-of-social-hygiene:
Havelock Ellis, the English writer on sex and society, set out his programme in The Task of Social Hygiene. Ellis says social hygiene grows out of the older idea of social reform, but goes deeper. Reform treated bad conditions as they arose. Hygiene, as he defines it, aims at prevention: finding the source of social ills before they take hold.

Ellis discusses the family, birth, education, and the health of the race. Some of his views carry the stamp of his age's faith in eugenics, which readers now judge harshly. Others look ahead to public health and planned welfare. The book is a clear statement of how one Edwardian thinker hoped science would remake society.
22097-byeways-in-palestine:
James Finn served as British consul in Jerusalem through the middle of the nineteenth century. His Byeways in Palestine gathers journeys off the beaten road of the Holy Land. Finn admits he carried no fine instruments, only sometimes a common thermometer. He had no time for digging or surveying; his consular work came first.

What he offers instead is close knowledge of the country and its peoples. Fellahin villages, Bedouin camps, Samaritan and Jewish communities all appear. Finn notices crops, ruins, customs, and quarrels with a resident's eye. The book is a useful record of Ottoman Palestine before tourists and archaeologists remade the picture of it.
22245-steve-and-the-steam-engine:
Sara Ware Bassett wrote Steve and the Steam Engine in 1921, a boys' novel with a railroad heart. Steve begins the book in disgrace. While his parents were in New York and the chauffeur lay in hospital, he took the family's big six-cylinder car without permission. He carried a crowd of friends to a football game at Torrington, and that, the narrator warns, was not the worst of it.

To earn back trust, Steve is sent to work where steam engines rule. Bassett's Cape Cod tales usually smell of salt water; here coal smoke takes over. The book teaches railroad practice inside a story of a boy making good. It is wholesome series fiction of the post-war years.
22317-george-bowring-a-tale-of-cader-idr:
George Bowring is R. D. Blackmore's tale of Cader Idris, drawn from Slain by the Doones. Cader Idris is the great Welsh mountain of legend. The story, though, opens with school days and a sudden parting.

Within a week, George and the narrator were forced to leave their school. They left the grand old town and the lovely Severn too. All they kept was one another. That loss hangs over the tale from its first pages. Blackmore blends boyhood friendship with Welsh mountain country. Readers get a short, fond, sorrowful story from a writer best known for the wilder Doone country nearby.
22470-the-bell-tone:
Edmund H. Leftwich wrote The Bell Tone, a science fiction story of alien signals. Its narrator studies a wave used for sending thought images. The wave measures .00176 meter, he reports with care.

Pictures may be sent with a clacking code or independently. The narrator can conceive no finer communications system than this. He resolves that he must learn their secret methods fully. That hunger to decode drives the tale's investigation of contact. Thought pictures cross space by tone in his account. Readers get an inventor's-eye tale of first contact by signal. It prizes clever decoding over battles or chases in space.
22511-rollo-on-the-rhine:
Jacob Abbott wrote Rollo on the Rhine for his famous Rollo travel series. Rollo tours Europe with his family, learning geography as he goes. This volume follows the great Rhine river country of Germany.

Abbott first explains how mountain waters find the sea. Thousands of smaller torrents unite into larger and larger streams. At length they make four mighty rivers of Europe. Streams of the southern slopes form one great river, the Po. It flows east into the Adriatic Sea, he teaches. Such lessons precede the castles and towns of the Rhine itself. Young readers learned Europe's rivers through a boy's journey. Abbott's calm, instructive voice made the series a household standard.
22833-alcyone:
Vast, empty space opens Alcyone, a long poem named for a bright star. Its opening crosses a lifeless waste where night rules alone, vast and still. Nothing lives there now. Only the crumbled remains of ancient worlds lie scattered through the silence.

From that cosmic graveyard the poem ranges over time, death, and the fate of worlds. Its manner is grand and solemn, closer to meditation than to story. Readers should expect sweeping questions rather than characters. The verse belongs to a period when astronomy fed poetry, and new knowledge of deep space stirred awe as much as fear. Alcyone preserves that awe in period dress.
23005-eli-first-published-in-the-century:
A boat needs painting in Eli, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. A boy comes down to the shore, and his father rises, surveying the green bottom of the boat. Mother sent word that dinner is ready, the father guesses. He must eat fast, he says, and finish painting the boat's far side before the tide turns.

Tide rules everything in Chaplin's fishing world, even dinner. His Eli is built from such small, true pressures, work against water, hunger against duty. The dialect stays light on the page and exact to the ear. Stories like this one made his name in the great magazines. They preserve the speech and labor of the New England shore, net by net and coat of paint by coat.
23006-five-hundred-dollars-first-publish:
Captains swap a story in Five Hundred Dollars, Heman White Chaplin's tale first published in the Century Magazine. Captain Bennett opens the yarn by recalling David Prince's whaling voyage on the Viola. Captain Philo agrees that Prince's departure, at the time, looked suspiciously hurried. With most anyone else, he'd have thought something was up.

Whaling money and a hurried departure promise the rest. Chaplin lets two old sailors unfold the tale at harbor pace, hint by hint. Five hundred dollars, the title's sum, hangs over Prince's voyage from the first exchange. The frame is half the pleasure, gnarled narrators weighing a younger man's luck. It is a yarn in the true sense, spun dockside.
23007-the-village-convict-first-publishe:
Snow crunches at the store door in The Village Convict, Heman White Chaplin's story first published in the Century Magazine. Trade's looking up, William, Captain Seth tells the storekeeper, as someone kicks snow off his boots on the doorstep. Somebody's found he's got to have a shoestring before morning, he jokes.

Inside that warm store waits the village's judgment on a man marked by prison. Chaplin's convict returns to a place where everyone knows his record and measures his worth by his work. The story asks how much mercy a small town keeps in stock. Its setting does quiet argument, neighbors talking a man's fate over in the ordinary run of trade. Chaplin handles the question without preaching.
23040-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for August 1866 argues about reunion. One essay imagines a statesman nearly despairing of the South after four years of war. Can anything good come from that quarter, he wonders. Yet a small, bright spot now shows at the Carolina cloud's very edge.

Hope and suspicion share this number, as they shared the country. Around the political essays sit poems, fiction, and reviews from the magazine's strong bench. The Atlantic stood at the center of American letters, and a monthly number shows its range in a single binding. August 1866 catches the nation mid-argument about what the war had settled. The spider's golden and silver silk of one image becomes, hopefully, a bond of union.
23108-chester-rand-or-the-new-path-to-fo:
Silas Tripp keeps the store in Chester Rand, or The New Path to Fortune. Silas Tripp may be Wyncombe's best-known citizen, the narrator figures. He runs the store in that Pennsylvania mountain village, lodges travelers in three spare rooms, serves as town treasurer, and fills other local offices besides.

Against Tripp's settled standing, young Chester Rand must find his path. Horatio Alger wrote this tale of a boy's rise, and its machinery is his, a good lad, a rich man to impress, luck that rewards virtue exactly on schedule. Store, town office, and mountain town fill the stage. Readers get the Alger formula in working order, cheerful, moral, and sure that fortune favors the deserving.
23137-diary-in-america-series-one:
Travelers contradict each other in Diary in America, series one. Talented travelers described the same nation in wildly clashing ways, the diarist marvels. Their harvests of fact, he adds, were generally meager for all their talent. The judgments pronounced on America, and pronounced so unjust by Americans, excited his curiosity.

Captain Frederick Marryat, the naval novelist, crossed the Atlantic to see for himself in the late 1830s. His diary records steamboats, prisons, elections, and manners with a sailor's bluntness. America fascinated and exasperated him by turns. Marryat's diary stands among the sharpest of the many British travel books on the young republic. Its author sized up a whole country with a naval officer's eye.
23246-mistress-anne:
Temple Bailey's Mistress Anne is a novel that opens in the afterglow of the holidays. The second day of the New Year fell on a Saturday, stretching the festive mood across the whole weekend. Wreaths from Christmas still hung in the windows. There had been an extra day of feasting, too.

Holidays always brought people in from town, Bailey notes, and they ate with sharp appetites. That warm, well-fed household sets the stage for Anne's story. Readers get a gentle period novel of home, guests, and manners, where small social moments carry the weight of the plot.
23292-ted-and-the-telephone:
Sara Ware Bassett's Ted and the Telephone, from 1922, is set in Freeman's Falls. Ted Turner lives in that sleepy New Hampshire town, beside a small river. Cotton mills stand in the town, and without them, Bassett notes, there would probably be no town at all.

The mills were not drawn to the town; the town arose because of the mills. That plain fact shapes Ted's world of work, family, and small-town ties. Readers get a novel of mill-town life in which a telephone, still a modern device, gives the story its title and its spark.
a-florentine-tragedy-la-sainte-courtisan:
Oscar Wilde left both of these verse plays unfinished, and they appear here in a 1917 Methuen volume of his miscellaneous works, with a preface explaining their history. A Florentine Tragedy is set in Renaissance Florence, where a merchant comes home to find his wife with a young noble. La Sainte Courtisane turns to the Egyptian desert, a holy hermit, and a beautiful courtesan.

In Florence, talk of cloth and money turns to swords before the night ends. In the desert piece, the hermit and the courtesan trade faith and desire in rich, strange speeches. Both fragments show Wilde reaching beyond drawing-room comedy toward dark, poetic drama, and both break off before completion.
a-rebellious-heroine:
John Kendrick Bangs plays a literary game in this tale from the 1896 Harper and Brothers edition, illustrated by W. T. Smedley. A novelist finds that the heroine he invented will not stay inside the story he planned for her. She has opinions about her own plot, her hero, and her author, and she acts on them.

The comedy runs on the collision between the author's intentions and his character's free will, a joke Bangs handles with the light touch of his House-Boat on the Styx. Chapters move between the writing desk and the world of the book. The piece is an early, cheerful example of fiction laughing at its own machinery.
a-ride-across-palestine:
Anthony Trollope tells how circumstances took him to the Holy Land without a companion, in this tale from the 1864 Tales of All Countries. He calls himself a gregarious animal, meant to go in pairs, and owns he was sad at heart in his Jerusalem hotel. Next morning he starts on horseback for the Dead Sea, Jordan, and Jericho.

Alone among strangers, he falls in with a fellow traveler whose company changes the ride, and the tale turns from sightseeing to character. Church of the Sepulchre, Mount of Olives, and Bethany pass by, but Trollope's interest is the living people on the road. The piece is travel writing worn as fiction, in his easy, confiding voice.
alone:
Norman Douglas wrote Alone as a book of travel sketches, most of them Italian, and dedicated it to his friend Edward Hutton. The contents run from Mentone and Levanto to Siena, Pisa, Viareggio, Rome, Olevano. Sorrento, with an introduction that looks back at the Great War and his comic failure to find patriotic employment in London offices.

Each place gets a loose essay of walks, inns, food, talk, and people met by the way, written in Douglas's dry, amused voice. Nothing is systematic: a town is a starting point for memory, argument, and appetite. Readers who know South Wind, named on his title page, will recognize the manner — a cultivated idler thinking aloud in Mediterranean sun.
anomalies-and-curiosities-of-medicine:
George M. Gould and Walter L. Pyle compiled this encyclopedic collection of medical anomalies. Its title page announces the scope: rare and extraordinary cases, and the most striking instances of abnormality in all branches of medicine and surgery. The material is drawn from medical literature from its origin to the present day, then abstracted, classified, annotated, and indexed.

The introductory essay argues that the anomalous has always driven science: monsters and strange growths show nature's workshop with its guard down. The body of the book then catalogs case after case from journals and older authors — unusual births, giant and dwarf growth, strange injuries survived, foreign bodies, and odd diseases. It became a standard sourcebook for physicians and, later, for writers of medical curiosities, valued for its citations as much as its wonders.
baby-mine: A popular play by Margaret Mayo about a wife who "borrows" a baby to win back her wandering husband, setting off a chain of comic mix-ups. A Broadway hit of 1910, it charmed audiences with its blend of farce and sentiment. This edition preserves a prime example of the light American comedy that packed theaters a century ago.
betty-zane: Zane Grey's 1903 first novel, based on his ancestress Elizabeth Zane, heroine of the siege of Fort Henry in 1782. Her famous run for gunpowder under Indian fire made her a frontier legend. Grey's tribute blends family history with rousing adventure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dunf: This 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia article on the Abbey of Dunfermline — burial place of Scottish kings, founded by St. Margaret — recounts its royal glory. Oswald Hunter-Blair gives its full story. A majestic reference on Scotland's Westminster. Bruce's heart, minus its crusade, rests in its choir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain: A 1913 entry on St. Augustine's, Canterbury — the apostle of England's own house. Rome's mission took root in Kent. George Cyprian Alston traces its story. Where English Christianity began. Its gate still greets pilgrims on the road to Canterbury. Ethelbert's tomb lies within its walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-bisho: A 1913 entry on Acacius of Caesarea — the Arian bishop who succeeded Eusebius. Cornelius Clifford tells his stormy story. Councils rose and fell around him. A prince of the losing side. His library preserved Origen's lost works. Jerome called him a one-eyed controversialist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-perse: A 1913 entry on Adam of Perseigne — the Cistercian abbot of mystical letters. Thomas Walsh praises his spiritual counsel. Kings and monks sought his advice. His letters breathe the cloister's peace. A director of souls in troubled times. His sermons on the Song of Songs are prized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonse-de-l: This 1913 reference article on Alphonse de Lamartine — the poet-statesman of France. Georges Bertrin weighs his fame and faith. His Méditations moved a generation. The 1848 republic heard his voice. France's singing statesman. His Jocelyn sang the priestly ideal. His fall was as swift as his rise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alsace-lorrai: This 1913 reference article on Alsace-Lorraine — the borderland's church story. Leo Ehrhard traces its sees through wars. France and Germany claimed its faith. Strasbourg's cathedral watched it all. A province between two empires. Its faith survived the changing flags. Its churches kept the French tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-stone: A 1913 entry on the altar stone — the consecrated slab with its relics. Augustin Schulte explains its necessity. Bishops seal the martyrs within. Missionaries carried such stones afar. The portable heart of the altar. Its cross is cut in the center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-wine: A 1913 entry on altar wine — the pure grape wine of the Mass. Augustin Schulte states the strict law. Only the vine's true juice suffices. Its care is the sacristan's trust. The chalice's worthy matter. Its cruet stands by the chalice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrogio-borg: This 1913 reference piece on Ambrogio Borgognone — the Lombard painter of quiet devotion. Augustus Van Cleef praises his altarpieces. His saints breathe a gentle piety. Milan's Certosa keeps his best. A master of the Lombard school. His frescoes glow in the Lombard chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce: A 1913 entry on Lindisfarne — the Holy Island of Aidan and Cuthbert. Columba Edmonds honors its golden age. The Gospels were painted in its scriptorium. harlequin-and-columbine: Booth Tarkington, twice winner of the Pulitzer Prize, lends his graceful style to this tale of love and the theater. Drawing on the old Italian comedy of Harlequin and his Columbine, the story follows romance through masks and misunderstandings. Tarkington's touch is light and humane, finding real feeling beneath the playfulness.
hebbel-herodes-und-mariamne:
Herod's jealous love for his wife Mariamne poisons his court, his reason, and finally her life. Hebbel's Herodes und Mariamne, given here in German, turns the biblical tyrant into a study of power corrupting love itself. Herod orders her death if he should fall, twice, rather than leave her to another man.

Suspicion feeds on silence, and silence feeds suspicion, until the trap closes. Mariamne's pride answers his with a fatal dignity of her own. Hebbel strips the old story to a pure clash of two unbending souls. The result is among the most intense psychological dramas in German. Few plays show so clearly how a ruler's love becomes his kingdom's curse.
honorine: Balzac's 1843 story of a husband's search for his runaway wife Honorine, and the quiet tragedy he uncovers. Tender, sad, and beautifully told, it is one of his most moving shorter works. The Human Comedy's study of a marriage.
john-keble-s-parishes-a-history-of-hursl:
John Keble's Parishes is Charlotte M. Yonge's history of Hursley and Otterbourne in Hampshire, printed in 1898. Yonge calls herself an old inhabitant of the place she describes. An earlier history by the Reverend John Marsh, curate of Hursley, appeared in 1808. Ninety years of change, she explains, made a fresh book needful.

Yonge keeps what she can of Marsh's careful work while adding new findings. She gives Otterbourne the fuller treatment Marsh denied it. The careers of John Keble, the clergyman and poet, and Sir William Heathcote stand at the center. She also records three churches built since 1837 and the parish changes around them. It is local history written from inside the parish.
legends-of-charlemagne:
Thomas Bulfinch retold the Legends of Charlemagne for general readers. The book forms part of his famous Bulfinch's Mythology. It stands beside The Age of Fable and The Age of Chivalry.

Charlemagne and his paladins ride through these medieval romances. Roland, Oliver, and other knights face Saracen armies and magic. Bulfinch smooths wild old poems into clear, lively prose. A publisher's preface praises his wide learning and patient care. Generations of readers first met Europe's legends in Bulfinch's retellings. Orlando's madness and Rinaldo's feats appear in these pages. Bulfinch keeps the marvels, yet trims the medieval sprawl.
life-and-adventures-of-calamity-jane:
Marthy Cannary, known as Calamity Jane, tells her own life story here. She says she was born in Princeton, Missouri, on May 1, 1852. Her family crossed overland to Virginia City, Montana, in 1865. The five-month trip filled her days with hunting and hard travel.

Jane recalls learning to ride the wildest horses while still a girl. She rode with the men whenever excitement or adventure offered itself. By the journey's end she was famed as a fearless rider and shot. Her plain-spoken memoir feeds the legend of the wild frontier West.
little-wars-a-game-for-boys-from-twelve-:
H. G. Wells explains his game of toy soldier battles here. Contents move from the legendary past to modern little warfare. Rules cover the country, the move, and each arm's mobility. Hand-to-hand fighting and capturing get their own sections.

The Battle of Hook's Farm shows the rules in action. Extensions and amplifications invite players to grow the game. An appendix compares Little Wars with the military Kriegspiel. Wells calls it the game of kings for humbler players. Soldier sizes and battle varieties receive practical sections. A sort of challenge ends the book's main text.
living-alone:
Stella Benson published this whimsical novel with Macmillan in 1920. A first edition had appeared the year before. Benson warns that this is not a real book at all. It does not deal with real people, she insists playfully.

Real books for real people already crowd the world, she jokes. Her little alien book serves the magically inclined minority. Chapters open with magic coming to a committee meeting. The committee then comes to magic in chapter two. The Pall Mall Gazette let Benson reprint her Mad 'Bus incident. An Athenæum poem called Detachment also joins the fifth chapter.
locrine:
This lamentable tragedy tells of Locrine, eldest son of Brutus. It discourses the wars of the Britains and the Huns. The Britains' victory and Locrine's death close its action. Five acts, each with a prologue, structure the play.

Ate, goddess of revenge, heads the list of persons. Scenes move between palaces, camps, riverbanks, and battlefields. The river afterward called the Humber recurs throughout. Catalogues credit Shakespeare, though scholars doubt his hand in it. Gwendoline's camp and Locrine's camp face each other in Act Five. An epilogue closes the tragedy after the field of battle.
lore-of-proserpine:
Lore of Proserpine is a 1913 book of tales and reflections by Maurice Hewlett. Its title names Proserpine, the queen of the dead in Greek myth. Hewlett writes about the fairy kind, who go where Fate drives them. Pieces here include 'The Windows,' 'A Boy in the Wood,' and 'Harkness's Fancy.'

The book mixes short tales with musings on an unseen world near our own. Hewlett treats fairies not as cute toys but as powers bound by Fate. His prose is dreamy and old-fashioned, full of woods, windows, and chance meetings. Readers who like folklore and fantasy will find a strange, quiet charm here. It stands apart from his better-known historical novels.
lorna-doone:
Lorna Doone is R. D. Blackmore's romance of Exmoor, published in 1869. Its hero is John Ridd, a strong and plain-spoken farmer. As a boy he meets Lorna, a girl held among the outlaw Doones. The Doones raid and rob across the moor, and their valley is feared by all.

John's love for Lorna grows as the feud between farmers and Doones deepens. The tale brings raids, rescues, and a fight for Lorna's freedom and name. Blackmore fills the book with moorland weather and old West Country ways. It became one of the best-loved English romances of its century. Its mix of love, danger, and landscape still draws readers.
margot-asquith-an-autobiography-two-volu: Margot Asquith wrote her own life story in this autobiography, issued by Project Gutenberg with both volumes joined in one text. The title page gives her name and the two-in-one form, and little more can be checked here. The hosted sample holds only the old Gutenberg header pages. This note therefore stays with the title facts and claims nothing about the memoir's contents.
married-life-its-shadows-and-sunshine:
Married Life; Its Shadows and Sunshine was printed at Philadelphia in 1852. T. S. Arthur wrote the book as a guide to a good marriage. His preface calls marriage the highest and purest bond in life.

Arthur says most strife comes from hasty and ill judged matches. He urges patience, kindness, and care for each other over pride. Couples who learn those habits, he argues, can turn a strained home toward peace. The preface frames the whole book as aid for homes in strain. Arthur writes for both the ill matched and the well matched pair.
mary-erskine:
Jacob Abbott wrote Mary Erskine as one of his Franconia stories. Harper printed it in New York in 1850. His preface lays out how he hoped such tales would shape young hearts.

Abbott says example moves a child far more than rules do. A kind word to a bird can plant kind ways for life. His tales show calm home scenes, with little direct preaching, and let the acts speak. The farm scene on the front page fits that calm aim. Franconia tales like this one taught through home life, not through fear.
master-sunshine:
Mrs. C. F. Fraser wrote Master Sunshine, a tale for young readers. Seven chapters run from Who He Was to A Happy Ending. The hero's real name is Frederick Alexander Norton, called Freddy.

His mother says he chose his bright name as a baby. His smiles and laugh spread cheer long before he could talk. His sister Lucy calls him buzzer, and the cook calls him an angel. Fraser shows his kind deeds on rainy days and Sundays at home. A rainy day, a Sunday with father, and brave deeds fill the heads. Each small act shows why the whole house leans on his cheer.
maurice-tiernay-soldier-of-fortune:
Charles James Lever wrote Maurice Tiernay, Soldier of Fortune, dated 1855. Downey of London reissued his novels in 1898, with pictures by A. D. McCormick. The heads start in the days of the guillotine.

A restaurant, the Temple prison, and the night of the ninth Thermidor follow. Tiernay must choose a life, then learn the army of sixty years past. A short scene in the record shows the poor home of Pere Michel. One small room, two chairs, and a charcoal pan made his whole hearth. A scrape and its results close the heads shown in the sample. Lever mixes camp life, Paris plots, and a young soldier's luck.
memories-of-hawthorne:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop published this family memoir in 1897. She was the daughter of novelist Nathaniel Hawthorne and his wife Sophia. Much of the book is built from Sophia's own letters, written from girlhood in 1820 until her death in 1871. Lathrop edited them into a portrait of both parents.

The opening chapters trace the Hawthorne and Peabody families and the couple's courtship. Readers meet Emerson and other Boston literary figures in passing. Lathrop writes plainly that few of her mother's pages deserved cutting. The result is an intimate record of a famous writer's home life, told by the family who lived it.
memories-of-jane-cunningham-croly-jenny-:
The Woman's Press Club of New York City published this memorial volume in 1904. It honors Jane Cunningham Croly, the journalist known by her pen name Jenny June. Caroline M. Morse edited the book. It is dedicated to the General Federation of Women's Clubs in America.

Inside are a brother's memories, speeches from a joint Sorosis and Press Club memorial meeting, and tributes from clubs across the country. Together they trace Croly's career in newspapers and her central role in the women's club movement. The volume shows how fellow writers and clubwomen judged her work while her influence was still fresh.
meyer-us4389981-hydrogen-gas-injector-sy:
United States Patent 4,389,981, granted to Stanley A Meyer on June 28, 1983, covers a hydrogen gas injector system for engines. Meyer claimed his water fuel cell split water into a burnable gas mix. The patent is one of eight in his water-fuel family held here.

The design feeds hydrogen gas into a standard engine in place of gasoline. Drawings and claims lay out the injector, its mix, and its controls in full legal detail. Patents prove a design was new on paper, not that it worked. In 1996 an Ohio court found Meyer's fuel claims fraudulent.
nasa-tm-19640007776-infrasonic-waves-fro:
Kaichi Maeda of Goddard Space Flight Center and Tomiya Watanabe wrote this paper. Watanabe was at the University of British Columbia. Their subject is infrasound, sound too low in pitch for ears to hear. Such waves had been linked with magnetic storms and auroras.

The authors propose that pulsing aurorae make these long pressure waves. Heating of the air near a set height is their favored mechanism. That height matches where auroral shimmering had been reported by others. The paper works out the energy links for the idea. It ties lights in the polar sky to slow waves that sensors can catch far away.
nasa-tm-19650019828-models-of-uranus-and:
Ray T Reynolds and Audrey L Summers, in the Space Sciences Division at Ames, built mathematical models of the planets Uranus and Neptune. No spacecraft had visited either planet. Their inner makeup had to be inferred from mass, size, and physics. The authors integrate basic balance equations on a computer to build self-consistent models.

They first estimate how likely materials behave at absolute zero. Then they plot mass against radius for model planets made of those materials. Sets of models for both planets follow from stated assumptions. The work shows what inner structures could fit the facts then known about two distant worlds.
nasa-tm-19660001387-compression-tests-on:
Lester Katz, in Marshall's Propulsion and Vehicle Engineering Laboratory, reported compression tests on cylinders stiffened as one piece in this August 6, 1965, memorandum. Such cylinders form the walls of rocket tanks and bodies. Under lengthwise load, a thin cylinder can buckle in two ways. It can fail as a whole, or wrinkle locally between stiffeners.

Katz determines the loads and stresses tied to each failure kind. Test results anchor the theory in real hardware behavior. Light, strong cylinders were vital to the Saturn program, where every pound of structure cost payload. Compression data like these told designers how thin they could safely go.
nasa-tm-19660011651-relativistic-charged:
Lawrence A Schmid at Goddard wrote this January 1966 paper, the third in a series on the flow of a charged fluid at near light speed. Part three builds a generalized Hamilton-Jacobi equation for that flow. A Clebsch transformation is applied to the problem, the catalog note says. Such equations are a compact way to state the laws that govern a moving plasma.

Relativistic plasma flow arises near extreme objects and in some fusion work. The mathematics is demanding, and each series part adds one tool. Schmid's paper is pure theory, aimed at specialists who model such flows. It shows Goddard's theoretical division working at the deep end of physics in support of space science.
nasa-tm-19670002002-mixing-and-reaction-:
Marshall C. Burrows, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for an aerospace sciences meeting in New York in January 1967. It studies how hydrazine and nitrogen tetroxide mix and react when fired against each other. The two liquids form a propellant pair that ignites on contact, so their mixing controls rocket chamber behavior.

Burrows used a quadlet injector element, with like propellant streams placed diagonally opposite at a right angle. Photographs showed the streams breaking into spray in less than an inch. Pockets of one propellant survived four inches or less downstream. Thermocouple readings showed the hottest gases in oxidizer-rich zones, while fuel-rich gases reflected hydrazine breaking down. Spectral measurements tracked water vapor and glowing gas bands, and products appeared well mixed eleven inches or more from the injector.
nasa-tm-19670022708-solar-power-systems-:
C. M. MacKenzie, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1967. It covers solar power systems for satellites in near-Earth orbits. Since Goddard's establishment in 1959, most of its satellites had drawn their primary electrical power from the Sun through silicon solar cells.

Solar cells alone, MacKenzie explains, often cannot deliver power at the right moments. Many orbits include eclipse periods with no sunlight at all. Other missions draw peak loads that sunlight alone cannot supply even in continuous illumination. Working systems therefore pair solar conversion with energy storage, batteries that carry the spacecraft through darkness and peaks. The paper describes several such systems in use at Goddard, including those of the IMP, Nimbus I, and ATS I satellites. Block diagrams show each system. A detailed section treats Explorer XXXIII's solar array, battery, and power control.
nasa-tm-19670027339-standard-for-color-c:
The Civil Engineering Division at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida issued this standard on February 21, 1967. Numbered KSC-STD-S-0003 and authenticated by division chief R. P. Dodd, it sets a color code for shop machinery and equipment. The standard was mandatory for the center and its associated contractors.

The code covers shop machines, tools, and similar equipment used in interior environments only. Color coding means any painting or refinishing, from a small touch-up to a complete repainting of an item. Its purpose is emphasis: bright color highlights hazardous or critical areas on a machine so personnel notice them. Equipment that other directives require to be coated with special compounds, for outdoor exposure, heat, cold, or acids, falls outside this standard. Referenced documents include a Navy color application manual, federal primer and enamel specifications, and the federal standard color list.
nasa-tm-19680008747-cooled-baffle-develo:
E. William Conrad, John P. Wanhainen, and Jerome K. Curley, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tamed a rocket part in this report. Baffles calm the combustion inside the M-1 engine, but they sit in brutal heat and must be cooled. The team developed cooled baffles using a smaller stand-in rocket.

The subscale engine matched the full M-1 in chamber pressure and mixture ratio. Its baffle compartment size also matched, so the heat environment was realistic. The team tested a long series of baffles with several cooling schemes. One design met the requirements with good durability. Transpiration-cooled baffles misbehaved unexpectedly and were ruled unsuitable.
nasa-tm-19680016292-measurements-of-the-:
Harold E. Taylor, K. W. Behannon, and N. F. Ness of Goddard Space Flight Center report magnetic field measurements behind the Moon in this paper. Explorer 35, in lunar orbit, measured the interplanetary magnetic field near the Moon. Explorer 33 made matching measurements away from the Moon at the same time.

The team found no shock waves in front of the Moon or close behind it. The field seemed to flow past the Moon with little distortion. A regular pattern of small ripples appeared inside the lunar wake, typically under three percent of the background field. Sharp field changes seen by Explorer 33 appeared nearly undistorted in the wake records.
nasa-tm-19690008659-results-of-magnetic-:
Masahisa Sugiura of Goddard Space Flight Center reviews magnetic surveys of the magnetosphere and nearby regions in this January 1969 paper. He presented it at an October 1968 symposium in Washington on describing Earth's magnetic field. The magnetosphere is the bubble of space ruled by Earth's magnetism, and spacecraft had only just mapped much of it.

Sugiura reports that the bubble's boundary and its outer bow shock shift position often. The tail behind Earth stays well defined eighty Earth radii out, and seems to persist a thousand radii back in wake-like form. A weak-field neutral sheet splits the tail's two halves. Storm-time ring currents and a quiet-time proton belt round out the survey.
nasa-tm-19700004913-d-region-radio-measu:
J. A. Kane of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this NASA technical memorandum in November 1968. It reports radio measurements of the D region made right at the magnetic equator. The D region is a low layer of the upper air, and its electrons change how radio waves travel.

Kane draws on two ARCAS rocket flights launched at Thumba, India, on March 8, 1968. Electron density profiles came from watching how much the radio signals faded as they crossed Earth's magnetic field. The introduction notes that mid-latitude results were already fairly well known, while equatorial ones were not. Steady weather near the equator also made it a clean place for the study.
nasa-tm-19700010501-an-improved-method-f:
James L. Zurasky of the Marshall Space Flight Center and Robert Forsten of Sperry Rand issued this report on January 5, 1970. It presents a sharper way to measure how thick a thin film is. Thin films are very shallow layers laid on a base, used in optical filters and electronic circuits.

The older method photographs light fringes from an interferometer and measures how far they shift at an etched step. That reading covered a wide area and gave accuracy of only about fifty to one hundred angstroms. The new method scans the photo negative with a microdensitometer instead. It uses only the sharpest small area, so fringe positions can be fixed far more closely.
nasa-tm-19700017797-microscopic-coupled-:
R. J. Ascuitto of Yale University led this study, with W. F. Ford and R. C. Braley of the Lewis Research Center and J. Bar-Touv of Ohio State University. They presented it at an American Physical Society meeting in April 1970. It models what happens when protons strike neon-20 nuclei.

In such hits, a proton can bounce off and leave the nucleus in a higher energy state. That outcome is called inelastic scattering. The team used a coupled-channel method, which tracks several possible outcomes at once. Their model works at the microscopic level, building the nucleus from its parts rather than treating it as a plain sphere.
nasa-tm-19700018037-the-generation-of-x-:
Klaus Schocken of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on February 12, 1970. It asks how planetary nebulae could give off X rays. A planetary nebula is a shell of gas shed by a dying star.

Schocken sums up how these nebulae evolve and how they produce radiation, drawing on published work. Their steady glow comes from free electrons losing energy near ions, he notes. That process explains their radio output and part of their visible light. If the nebulae also emit X rays, he argues, the same process would most likely make them.
nasa-tm-19700026472-mission-training-pro:
The Mission Training Section at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this internal note. It sets out the training program for the third crewed Apollo mission. The section's chief, Jon J. Van Boekel, signed the program, which crews followed for months on simulators and checklists before they flew.

One strand puts crew members inside real spacecraft tests as participants, not just observers. Another strand runs the briefings, reviews, and meetings that fill the schedule between practice flights. Separate briefing series cover the command and service module systems and the lunar module systems. Launch vehicle and guidance program briefings follow, along with photography and the extravehicular mobility unit, the backpack suit system.
nasa-tm-19700030449-the-prediction-of-co:
K. H. Schatten of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in September 1970. It treats the prediction of magnetic fields in the Sun's corona and in the space between the planets. Those fields shape the solar wind and can disturb radio links and spacecraft far from the Sun.

Fast computers and better solar knowledge, Schatten notes, had made eclipse structure predictions possible. He discusses the magnetic field models behind such forecasts, their uses, and their limits. Solar activity's effect on coronal shape gets its own treatment. Recent work by other solar researchers, showing the surface field tracks the field between planets, points to a practical way of forecasting that wider field.
nasa-tm-19710005374-optimization-of-self:
Bernard J. Hamrock and David P. Fleming of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a March 1971 gas bearing meeting in Southampton, England. It finds the best designs for self-acting herringbone journal bearings. The goal is the greatest radial load the bearing can carry.

A computer program worked out the optimal bearing for each case. The authors turn the results into design curves that cover a wide range. The curves span calm, thick gas films and highly squeezed ones. Either the smooth part or the grooved part may be the one that turns. Bearings of this kind serve in fast, clean machines where oil cannot go.
nasa-tm-19710021715-the-nasa-quiet-engin:
James J Kramer of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a fall 1971 engineering meeting in Los Angeles. It introduces the NASA Quiet Engine Program. The program folded all known noise reduction methods into one propulsion system. The target was a power plant fit for subsonic civil transport aircraft. Jet noise had become a public and political problem by then.

Full scale experimental hardware was being built for the program. Tests focused mainly on noise performance, not thrust. Kramer reported the program as still in progress. Component tests finished so far pointed in an encouraging direction. The work aimed to prove a complete quiet engine, not just quiet parts. Airlines and regulators both watched for usable results.
nathaniel-hawthorne:
George E. Woodberry wrote this life of Nathaniel Hawthorne, the American novelist and story writer. Woodberry dated his preface at Columbia College on April 1, 1902. He built the book from Hawthorne's own writings, his note books, and family accounts by his son, daughter, and son in law.

Chapters move from Hawthorne's first years to the chamber under the eaves where he wrote. Later chapters cover his work as weigher and gauger, the Old Manse years, and The Scarlet Letter. Woodberry also thanks friends who let him quote their own memories. The result is a careful early life of a major American author.
nocturne:
Frank Swinnerton dated his Nocturne December 1917, and dedicated it to Martin Secker. The contents divide the tale by hours, like music played at night. Part one is Evening, with chapters named Six O'Clock, The Treat, Rows, and The Wish. The shape promises one night told in full.

Part two, Night, brings The Adventure, The Yacht, and Mortals. Penalties and What Followed lead to a chapter called Cinderella. Part three is Morning, starting with After the Theatre. Swinnerton lets a single night carry love, risk, and shame, then shows the morning after. The contents alone trace a fall and a reckoning.
old-cookery-books-and-ancient-cuisine:
William Carew Hazlitt wrote this history of old cooking in 1902. It appeared in the Book-Lover's Library series in London. Hazlitt begins by noting man's dislike of raw food. He contrasts human cooking with the habits of animals. Fruit, salads, and oysters form rare exceptions, he says.

The book surveys old cookery books and early ways of eating. Hazlitt writes with humor about game kept until very ripe. He traces taste, custom, and table manners over centuries. Food lovers gain a guide to early recipe books. The work blends food history with bookish charm.
old-times-at-otterbourne:
Charlotte Mary Yonge wrote this village history in 1891. Warren and Son printed the second edition in Winchester. Otterbourne is a Hampshire parish near the River Itchen. Yonge feared the oldest memories would soon be lost. She records life before railroad, church, and penny post.

She traces a Roman road and a Roman medallion there. The name likely means village of the otters, she says. Saxon kings, bishops, and parish bounds shape the story. The metadata note stresses her church faith and huge output. The book preserves local memory in warm, careful detail. It suits readers of English village history.
on-the-firing-line:
Anna Chapin Ray and Hamilton Brock Fuller wrote this novel. Chapter one opens aboard a ship at sea. Harvard Weldon is tall, broad, and sure of himself. He pursues talk with his table neighbor, Ethel Dent. She answers him with dry, cool indifference at first.

Weldon has spent three days trying to break her reserve. A careless waiter first gave him his opening chance. Her chaperon, Miss Arthur, lies horribly seasick nearby. Its title points from shipboard flirtation toward war. Ray writes bright dialogue with a romantic edge. He jokes that a past football hurt once broke his collar bone. Mild walks after lunch are his doctor's firm advice, he adds.
over-the-border-acadia-the-home-of-evang: Eliza B. Chase's Over the Border is a travel and history book about Acadia. Longfellow made that Nova Scotia country famous as Evangeline's home. The hosted sample shows the title page, contents, and a chronology's start only. The contents promise the Bay of Fundy and the Basin of Minas. Port Royal, Halifax, and Grand Pré follow. The chronology opens in 1604. No narrative page appears.
patriarchal-palestine:
A. H. Sayce, professor of Assyriology at Oxford, wrote Patriarchal Palestine for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. The book studies the land of the Bible in the age of the patriarchs. A map at the front marks the chief places named in Genesis and Exodus.

Sayce tests the biblical picture against the records of Egypt and Assyria. The text works through Egyptian king lists, including the dynasties reported by Manetho, and the wars of Theban princes. His aim is to show what archaeology and ancient inscriptions can confirm, correct, or add to the story told in Genesis.
podcast-tuckercarlson-L28k2FTSENE:
Doctor Mary Talley Bowden is a Texas physician who clashed with her hospital and regulators during the Covid years. She joins Tucker Carlson to argue that vaccines became politicized. She also argues that the medical industry destroyed its own credibility in the process. Her account is personal as well as polemical: she describes being punished for her treatment choices and public statements.

Carlson treats her story as a case study in institutional coercion. Bowden's views on Covid treatment remain contested by the medical mainstream, and her claims are preserved here as her own. The episode documents a real rift: doctors who believe the profession traded trust for obedience, speaking to an audience that largely agrees. Listeners can hear the dissenting physicians' movement explain itself, in the voice of one of its most litigated members.
poems-by-emily-dickinson-series-one:
Emily Dickinson published almost nothing while she lived, and the first series of her Poems introduced her work to the public after her death. Dickinson wrote in seclusion at her family home in Amherst, Massachusetts, packing short, intense lyrics with dashes, slant rhymes, and startling images of nature, death, and faith. Only a handful of her poems appeared in print before she died, out of nearly eighteen hundred found among her papers.

Editors prepared this first volume from her manuscripts so that friends and curious readers could finally meet the work whole. The shock of the style was part of the event: hymns bent out of shape, thoughts compressed to a few lines, a voice unlike any other in American poetry. Every later Dickinson collection builds on the opening this series made.
poems-of-paul-verlaine:
Paul Verlaine's poems appear in English in this volume translated by Gertrude Hall and pictured by Henry McCarter, with a portrait of the poet at the front. Verlaine, the French symbolist whose musical, melancholy verse reshaped modern poetry, is represented by his three most famous early collections. Hall's translations keep the French titles for the sections while rendering the poems themselves into English song.

Fêtes Galantes opens the book, with Clair de Lune, Mandoline, and the Colloque Sentimental, moonlit scenes of lovers in powdered dress. La Bonne Chanson follows, love poems written for a young fiancée, all hearth light and summer days. Romances sans Paroles closes with the wordless songs, including the famous poem where it weeps in his heart like rain on the city. English readers of the period met the essential Verlaine in this handsome, illustrated form.
proportional-representation-applied-to-p:
T. R. Ashworth and H. P. C. Ashworth proposed a new electoral system in a book printed in London by Swan Sonnenschein in 1901. The elder Ashworth led the Victorian branch of an Australian free trade and liberal group.

Chapters set out the true rules of representation and attack the faults of party government. Two plans are then detailed, the Hare system and the free list system, both built on delegation in line with votes. A closing chapter applies the reform to Australian law-making bodies. Readers get a full scheme for fairer voting.
quincy-adams-sawyer-and-mason-s-corner-f:
Quincy Adams Sawyer and Mason's Corner Folks, a picture of New England home life by Charles Felton Pidgin, was published at Boston by C. M. Clark Publishing Company in 1905 in a revised edition. Pidgin dedicates the book to the memory of James Russell Lowell, whose poem The Courtin' gave him the idea for the story.

In his preface Pidgin notes that his hero's only title is plain "Mr.," though his ancestors were tradesmen, merchants, lawyers, politicians, and Presidents. He aims to make Quincy live up to an ideal of gentlemanly qualities, and argues that the New England standard for a novel's hero should stand as high as Old England's.
quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of-mich:
Quotes and Images from Michel de Montaigne takes its quotations from the five volumes of the Essays, with five etchings promised at the head of the selection. David Widger sets the great French essayist's sentences in alphabetical order, a Montaigne for browsing.

A child should not be brought up in his mother's lap, and a generous heart ought not to belie its own thoughts. A man may govern himself well who cannot govern others, may play the fool in everything but poetry, and never speaks of himself without loss. A little cheese makes a feast when the mind is set, and a well-bred man is a compound man.
real-soldiers-of-fortune:
Richard Harding Davis profiles men who fought for hire or for causes not their own, and his book opens with Major-General Henry Ronald Douglas MacIver. MacIver may be met, Davis says, on Fifth Avenue, gray-haired and stiffly erect, with a sabre cut across his forehead. His titles ran from ensign in India to general of brigade in Servia.

Born at sea off Virginia on Christmas Day, 1841, MacIver was schooled at Edinburgh and sent to India at sixteen. He fought in the Indian Mutiny, took a sword cut through helmet and towel into his skull, and was left for dead. He next wore Garibaldi's red shirt in Italy, and few later wars lacked him.
reymont-the-comedienne:
Wladyslaw Reymont tells of a young woman who flees dull town life in The Comedienne, here in English. She joins a traveling theater troupe, hungry for art and fame. Backstage life soon shows her both its glitter and its grime.

Reymont, later a Nobel laureate, knew poverty and striving at first hand. His heroine pays for ambition with pride, love, and hard lessons. The troupe's actors, jealous, kind, and vain, ring true in every scene. The novel gives a vivid, unsparing portrait of artistic dreams in partitioned Poland, and of the price a woman paid to chase them.
rhymes-of-a-rolling-stone:
Robert W. Service gathered these verses in a book first issued in 1912, here in a printing of 1917. A comic verse at the front begs pardon for his literary sins, saying the other kind do not matter. A prelude and a title poem, A Rolling Stone, open the contents.

The Soldier of Fortune, The Gramaphone at Fond-Du-Lac, and Athabaska Dick carry the northern settings of his fame. Sunshine, Cheer, Ambition, and Dreams Are Best strike his hopeful note. Darker pieces stand beside them: The Blind and the Dead, Death in the Arctic, and The Lunger. Barb-Wire Bill and The Rover keep the wandering figure of the title in view throughout.
rodney-stone:
A. Conan Doyle's Rodney Stone appears here in an edition from Eveleigh Nash and Grayson of London, dated 1921. Doyle's preface, signed at Haslemere on September 1, 1896, lists the books he drew on for life in England at the start of the century. Gronow's Reminiscences, Jesse's Life of Brummell, and Fitzgerald's Life and Times of George the Fourth stand among them.

Boxiana and Pugilistica fed the prize-ring scenes, and Doyle thanks Robert Barr and J. C. Parkinson for facts on the ring. Harper's Brighton Road, Rice's History of the Turf, and naval lives of Collingwood and Nelson complete his shelf. Contents open at Friar's Oak, with Buck Tregellis, the Peace of Amiens, and the Brighton Road ahead.
ronicky-doone:
Max Brand published this western novel in 1921, opening at a gallop in its first chapter, A Horse in Need. A rider comes into town inside a solid cloud of dust, his horse at the last limit of strength. Dull eyes, hanging head, and sweat dripping into the white street dust mark the animal's state.

The rider is nearly as spent, a wide-shouldered, gaunt man with dust masking his face and pink skin round his eyes. He climbs the hotel steps and asks the loungers for a horse to reach Stillwater within three hours' riding. The oldest man answers first, this being a matter of life and death: any horse can do it, by the short way across the mountain.
salomy-jane: Bret Harte wrote Salomy Jane, with pictures by Harrison Fisher and Arthur I. Keller, issued at Boston and New York in 1910 by Houghton Mifflin. Copyrights of 1898, 1900, and 1910 stand on the title page. The contents list four chapters: A Kiss and an Escape, The Lady's Reflections, The Kiss Repeated, and Another Escape. The first chapter heading is repeated at the close of the pages shown here, with no narrative passage following it in this portion.
sane-sex-life-and-sane-sex-living-some-t:
H. W. Long, M.D., wrote Sane Sex Life and Sane Sex Living, an authorized edition issued in New York in 1919 by the Eugenics Publishing Company. The subtitle promises things that all sane people ought to know about sex nature and sex functioning, its place in the economy of life, its proper training, and its righteous exercise. Long gives the volume to fellow members of the medical profession and to all who may read it under their direction. A firm note asks that the book be read from beginning to end without skipping, at least on a first reading, if its purpose is to be realized.

The contents outline that purpose in plain heads. An explanatory introduction charges that wrong teachings about sex leave children brought up in ignorance on sex matters.
sanine: Michael Artzibashef wrote Sanine, translated by Percy Pinkerton with a preface by Gilbert Cannan. The contents page shown here gives press notices of the novel in place of a chapter list. The New Statesman finds a treble interest: sex problems discussed with unusual candour, a vivid picture of Russian life, and the welter of thoughts common to the whole contemporary Western world.
sarrasine:
Honore de Balzac wrote Sarrasine, presented here in English by Clara Bell and others and dedicated to Charles Bernard du Grail. The story begins near midnight at a grand Paris house party. From a curtained window seat the narrator watches two scenes at once and sets them against each other.

Outside, snow rests on the garden trees under a cloudy, moonlit sky, and the pale shapes suggest ghosts and death. Inside, well-dressed guests fill a bright salon where jewels, music, talk, and card play hold attention. The narrator lingers on the contrast between the cold, quiet garden and the warm, crowded rooms before the tale moves on.
seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-volume:
Francis W. Halsey edited this third volume of his ten-volume travel set, opening France and the Netherlands in Part One. The tourist bound for France lands at Cherbourg, Havre, or Boulogne, each port rich in recalled events. Cherbourg recalls the sea fight where the Kearsarge sank the Alabama.

An opening survey runs from Roman rule in Gaul through the growth of great ports like Marseilles. Famed writers then lead readers through towns, churches, and coast scenes. The volume pairs trip guidance with deep history, so a traveler lands knowing the ground's long past as well as its present face.

Francis W. Halsey edited this fourth volume of his travel set in 1914, carrying France and the Netherlands into Part Two. The volume centers on cathedrals and chateaux, the great church and castle sites of France. Named guides include Thomas Frognall Dibdin, H. A. Taine, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.

Contents list Bayeux and its famed tapestry, the chateau of Henry IV at Pau, and Loire valley seats such as Amboise, Blois, and Chambord. Each stop pairs a building's stones with the tales and rulers tied to it. Art and history lovers get a rich route through old France.
since-ce-zanne:
Clive Bell gathered these art essays around the change Cezanne wrought in modern painting. Contents move from the artistic problem and the Douanier Rousseau to Renoir, then to tradition and movements. Matisse and Picasso share a chapter, while Bonnard and Duncan Grant receive their own.

Portraits of Cezanne, Seurat, Matisse, and Picasso stand among the pictures. Later essays treat Negro sculpture, standards, and art's place in criticism, closing with jazz and M. Derain's authority. Bell writes as a champion of the new French art, arguing that form, not story, gives a picture its life.
soldiers-of-fortune:
Richard Harding Davis opens his novel Soldiers of Fortune in a New York drawing room. Mrs. Porter begs Alice Langham to come early and do her a favor at dinner. A man she barely knows needs a place at the table, and the debutantes, she says, grow cross when set next to men who cannot help them. Alice, known as good-natured, is her hope.

The guest is a cowboy friend of George's, met while shooting in New Mexico or Old Mexico. He fed George, gave him game to shoot, and now calls in New York with a letter asking to be placed. Mrs. Porter will set him next to Alice, with Reginald King on her other side. Alice's look of fun cools at King's name, and she grants the plan with stiff grace.
sterne:
H. D. Traill published his life of Sterne in 1882, working with sources he admits are thin. For the years before fame, nearly all that survives is a short memoir Sterne wrote for his daughter. He wrote it a few months before his death. It covers childhood, school days, Cambridge, and his Yorkshire vicarage.

From 1759 onward, Sterne's letters run to 1768, the year he died, and form the main record of his later life. Traill weighs the earlier attempts too. He treats Scott's brief memoir and Thackeray's lecture essay. He also credits Percy Fitzgerald's two large volumes with holding nearly all the facts now likely to be recovered. Those facts concern the author of Tristram Shandy and the Sentimental Journey.
stifter-bunte-steine:
Each story in Stifter's Bunte Steine takes its name and mood from a stone: granite, limestone, tourmaline, and others. Colored Stones, given here in German, gathers tales of family, fate, and the Austrian landscape. Children in danger and parents in prayer recur across the collection's quiet dramas.

Precise, luminous, and morally serious, the stories rank among the finest short works in German. A plague year, a mountain rescue, a foundling's fate: small events carry enormous weight in Stifter's hands. Nature is never mere scenery; it tests and shelters his people in turn. The collection makes the essential Stifter for the short-story reader. Few books prove so well that gentleness and power can share a style.
stories-from-everybody-s-magazine: Only the front pages of an old electronic text are present here. They announce stories drawn from the 1910 issues of Everybody's Magazine, dated October 1996, and carry the standard welcome and donation appeals of that early free-text project. No title page, contents list, or story text from the magazine itself appears in these opening pages.
stories-from-the-pentamerone:
Giambattista Basile's tales, known as Il Pentamerone, were first published at Naples in the Neapolitan dialect. A note at the front says Basile, Count of Torrone, is believed to have gathered the tales chiefly in Crete and Venice, and to have died about the year 1637.

The contents list thirty-two pieces, from How the Tales Came to Be Told through The Myrtle, Peruonto, The Flea, and Cenerentola, an early form of the Cinderella story. Serpents, enchanted does, dragons, the tale of Sun, Moon, and Talia, and The Three Citrons follow. These rough, witty folk tales stand among the first great printed collections in Europe.
story-of-chester-lawrence-being-the-comp:
Nephi Anderson's Story of Chester Lawrence came from The Deseret News at Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1913. It completes the account of a man who played an important part in his earlier novel. That novel was Piney Ridge Cottage. Anderson's other books include Added Upon and The Castle Builder.

The tale opens in rain at a pier, where a crowd under dripping umbrellas waves farewell to friends aboard a departing ship, and a late passenger scrambles up with heavy hand baggage. Anderson wrote fiction rooted in his Mormon faith and Utah life, and this story follows Chester Lawrence beyond the earlier book, giving his part of the tale in full at last.
sue-a-little-heroine: Only the opening pages are present here. They give a title page for Sue, A Little Heroine, by L. T. Meade, printed by the New York Book Company in 1910, followed by a publisher's biography of the author. That sketch names her as Mrs. Elizabeth Thomasina Smith, born at Bandon, County Cork, in 1854, a first book written at seventeen, and more than fifty novels after, many drawn from her studies of East London life. No page of Sue's own story appears here.
tattine:
Ruth Ogden, who also wrote as Mrs. Charles W. Ide, made Tattine a tale for young readers, built around a small girl and her dogs. Chapter one is called Trouble No. 1, and trouble is the heart of the book.

Tattine, age seven, sits in an apple tree one June morning, sketching a chime tower on a neighbor's land. Below her rest her setters Betsy and Doctor, while Doctor's granddam Tadjie lies buried near by. That day Tattine learns that some wrongs lie past even her mother's power to set right. Readers get a soft, grave child's tale about loss, love of pets, and the first hard truths of life.
tempest-and-sunshine:
Mary J. Holmes wrote Tempest and Sunshine, a novel in twenty-six chapters printed by J. H. Sears and Company of New York. Chapter one is headed Mr. Wilmot Arrives at Mr. Middleton's, and the scene is set in Kentucky.

On a bright October day at four, the Lexington and Frankfort stage rattles into the small town of V, drawn by four tired horses. It halts at The Eagle, the chief hotel of the place, as a guest steps down. Readers enter a tale of two unlike sisters, hinted by the title's storm and sun, in a once-loved American novel of love, pride, and family strife in the South.
that-fortune:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote That Fortune, a novel that starts with a boy of twelve and a tall tree on a mountain edge. Chapter one lingers on that perch before the tale moves out into the world.

The lad swings in the top of a lithe hickory, the first picket of a forest, above rocky pasture and chestnut woods. Below run orchards, cornfields, and an amber river whose murmur climbs to him like an old tale he cannot yet grasp. The wind's push and the tree's spring stir him, and ambition to make his own way stirs too. Readers follow Philip Burnett from this hilltop into wealth, law, and love, in a tale of what fortune does to a man.
the-32nd-mersenne-prime-predicted-by-mer:
